transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
I'm here because I've been struggling with episodes where I eat an unusually large amount of food. When this happens, I feel like I completely lose control and just can't seem to stop eating.
After these eating episodes, do you do anything to try to prevent weight gain, like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising excessively?
No, I don't do any of those things at all. I've never tried to make myself throw up, use laxatives, or do any extreme fasting or exercising to make up for the eating.

During these episodes, do you also eat much more quickly than usual, eat until you feel uncomfortably full, eat when you’re not physically hungry, or feel disgusted, depressed, or very guilty afterward?

Yes, I definitely eat much faster than normal during those times, and I do it even when I'm not physically hungry at all. Afterwards, I just feel incredibly guilty, depressed, and disgusted with myself.
How often have these binge-eating episodes been happening, and has this been going on for at least 3 months?
Yes, this has been going on for about three or four months now. It happens at least once a week on average, sometimes even more frequently than that.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Binge-Eating Disorder"], and based on this conversation the list remains the same because the patient describes recurrent binge-eating episodes with loss of control, associated features (eating rapidly, eating when not hungry, marked guilt/depressed/disgusted feelings afterward), occurring at least weekly for 3-4 months, and denies compensatory behaviors. This strongly supports Binge-Eating Disorder and does not suggest Bulimia Nervosa or Anorexia Nervosa.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent episodes of eating an unusually large amount of food with loss of control, associated features of rapid eating, eating when not physically hungry, and marked guilt/depressed/disgusted feelings afterward. Episodes occur at least weekly for 3–4 months, and the patient denies compensatory behaviors, supporting Binge-Eating Disorder.
